“Good-bye, Uncle George. If I linger any longer, I shall be late for luncheon. Thank you for the information I came for. I always prefer to know everything about new friends and nothing about old ones.”

“Where do you lunch, Harry?”

“With Aunt Agatha. I have invited myself and Mr. Gray. He is the latest of her protégés.”

“Humph! Tell your Aunt Agatha to stop troubling me with appeals for charity, Harry. I am thoroughly tired of them. The good woman seems to imagine I have no occupation beyond writing cheques for her foolish enthusiasms.”

“Certainly, Uncle George, I shall tell her, but it will achieve nothing. Philanthropists lose every feeling of humanity. That is their characteristic mark.”

The old gentleman gave an approving growl and rang for his servant. Lord Henry went along the low arcade into Burlington Street and directed his steps towards Berkeley Square.

So this was the history of Dorian Gray's birth. Roughly related though it had been, it moved him with the hint of a curious, almost modern romance. A lovely woman staking all upon a reckless passion. A few delirious weeks of happiness ended by a dreadful, treacherous crime. Months of silent anguish, followed by a child born in suffering. Death carrying off the mother, and the boy abandoned to loneliness and the dominion of an old man without love. Yes, a compelling background. It gave the lad a setting, rendered him more perfect, one might say. Behind every exquisite thing lay some tragedy. Worlds must endure labour-pains before the humblest flower could bloom.... And how delightful he had been at dinner the previous evening, sitting opposite him at the club with astonished eyes and lips opening in a pleasure almost fearful, while the red candle-shades deepened to rose the awakening wonder in his face. Conversation with him resembled playing a beautiful violin. Every touch and tremor of the bow found its response.... The act of influencing another held a terrible fascination. Nothing else compared with it. To cast one's soul into a lovely shape and allow it to remain there briefly; to hear one's intellectual convictions returned with the additional music of youth and passion; to pour one's temperament into another as if it were a delicate liquid or an unfamiliar perfume—there was authentic delight in that. Perhaps it was the most complete delight remaining in an age as narrow and vulgar as their own, an age crudely sensual in its enjoyments and crudely commonplace in its ambitions.... This lad, whom a strange accident had brought to him in Basil's studio, was a magnificent type as well—or, at least, might be moulded into one.

I therefore went to the plantation and resumed my questions among the older Black people there. Eventually, one of the oldest women said she had heard of a place called Bessop's Castle and believed she could lead me to it. It was neither a castle nor a tavern, she explained, but a tall rock.

“I offered to pay her generously for the trouble, and after some hesitation she agreed to take me there. We found the spot without much difficulty. After sending her away, I began to examine it. The ‘castle’ was an irregular cluster of cliffs and rocks, one of which stood out for its height and its isolated, apparently artificial shape. I climbed to its summit and then found myself uncertain what to do next.

“As I considered the problem, I noticed a narrow ledge on the rock's eastern face, perhaps a yard below the summit where I stood. It projected about eighteen inches and measured no more than a foot across. A hollow in the cliff immediately above gave it a rough resemblance to one of the recessed-back chairs our ancestors used. I had no doubt that this was the ‘devil's seat’ mentioned in the manuscript, and now the whole secret of the riddle seemed within my grasp.

“I knew that ‘a good glass’ could mean only a telescope, since sailors rarely use the word ‘glass’ in any other sense. I immediately understood that I was to use a telescope here, from a precisely fixed viewpoint that allowed no variation. I also felt certain that ‘forty-one degrees and thirteen minutes’ and ‘northeast and by north’ gave the directions for aiming it. Greatly excited by these discoveries, I hurried home, obtained a telescope, and returned to the rock.

“I lowered myself onto the ledge and discovered that I could remain seated only in one particular position. This confirmed my earlier assumption. I then began using the telescope. Clearly, ‘forty-one degrees and thirteen minutes’ could refer only to the elevation above the visible horizon, because ‘northeast and by north’ already specified the horizontal direction. I found that direction at once with a pocket compass. Then, aiming the telescope upward at as close to forty-one degrees as I could estimate, I carefully adjusted it higher and lower. At last my attention was caught by a round gap or opening in the leaves of a large tree that rose above the others in the distance.

Their coming had kindled something like a fire in Saint Antoine's breast, spreading swiftly as they advanced, and stirring and flickering in the flames of faces at nearly every window and door. Nevertheless, nobody had followed them, and not a man spoke when they came into the wine-shop, although every man's eyes were fixed upon them.

“Good day, gentlemen!” Monsieur Defarge said.

Perhaps this was a signal to release the general tongue. A chorus of “Good day!” answered him.

“The weather is bad, gentlemen,” said Defarge with a shake of his head.

At this each man glanced at his neighbour; then all lowered their eyes and remained silent. All except one, who rose and left.

“My wife,” Defarge said aloud to Madame Defarge, “I have come several leagues with this worthy mender of roads, whose name is Jacques. I met him—by chance—a day and a half's journey from Paris. This road-mender called Jacques is a good fellow. Give him something to drink, my wife!”

A second man rose and left. Madame Defarge placed wine before the road-mender called Jacques, who removed his blue cap to the company and drank. Some coarse brown bread was tucked into the breast of his blouse; from time to time he ate a little, sitting near Madame Defarge's counter and munching between draughts. A third man rose and left.

Defarge revived himself with a drink of wine, though he took a smaller portion than the stranger had received, since for him it was no uncommon treat. He stood waiting for the countryman to finish breakfast. He glanced at nobody in the room, and nobody now glanced at him, not even Madame Defarge, who had resumed her knitting and was busily employed.

“Have you completed your meal, friend?” he asked when the time came.

“Yes, thank you.”

“Then come! I will show you the lodging I said you might have. It will suit you wonderfully.”

From the wine-shop to the street, from the street to a courtyard, from the courtyard up a steep stair, from the stair into a garret—the very garret where a white-haired man had once bent forward upon a low bench, absorbed in making shoes.

The white-haired man was no longer there. Instead stood the three men who had left the wine-shop one by one. Their sole small connection with that distant white-haired man was that they had once peered at him through cracks in the wall.

Defarge shut the door with care and lowered his voice.

“Jacques One, Jacques Two, Jacques Three! Here is the witness whom I, Jacques Four, met by arrangement.
